commentBody: Nicely challenging.
Playful, clean, tight, entertaining. Quick. Thanks to KAC.

When steak tartare goes on sale, it's a raw deal.

(That pun's hardly well done.)

Well that might the best 1A clue and answer I’ve ever seen. 

Wonderful puzzle! Thanks muchly!
1A had me roaring once I figured it out. The funnest crossword clue I've ever encountered. Thank you for such an enjoyable puzzle.

Fort HAYS tripped me up. Probably saw road signs for it last week on my way from Dodge City to Nicodemus National Historic Site. Looks like, it would have been the fork at Wa Keeney.

Also, I'm not convinced the constructor of the Midi has actually ever played Tic Tac Toe. It the theme is going to be a three by three TTT grid, it ain't work like that

Ooh, that was a nice puzzle. Parsing C DRI_E (for a 20-year-now Mac user) crossing _ERE (“C’mon high school reading synapse, fire, *fire*!) ended in the walk-of-shame running of the alphabet, but everything else fell into place—thankfully, not too quickly, but after a nice workout. 

Might’ve been quicker if I weren’t being eaten alive by a hungry beyond reason mosquito which has been buzzing (and strafing the troops on the ground) in my room for a couple of hours now. I have no flyswatter; I can’t roll up my digital NY Times into a weapon. All I can do is go through a whole tube of antihistamine cream and listen to Señor Gato snore blissfully from under his fortress of fluffiness. God I miss the high desert. 

Have a good Saturday, everyone.
KAC always delivers. Fun puzzle.
Just right for Saturday.  Bravo

YOU ARE HERE: in the midst of a KAC creation. CRIKEY you may say, or NOW WHAT?
UPPER VOLTA to the rescue!  All HALCYON now.

Now this is the Kameron Austin Collins we know and love!  (Well, at least I do).

I admit I kind of flew through this, not because I thought it was easy but because I was having so much darned fun! I didn’t stop on any one thing, just jumped around and seemed to be channeling Kameron’s mind in a few places. 

I admit UPPERVOLTA and DIANFOSSEY, the twin Africa clues today, really got me a foothold—not my usual speciality. I don’t know if I’ve ever seen IRENEPAPAS but somehow the name  was cowering in the recesses of my mind.

You had me at BATARANGS.

ESTATESALE, AVIDREADER, BALDISH, and STRESSEATS are instant classics and the kind of clueing we expect from KAC.

A few wrong turns for me—I had CANTSTOPIT before CANTHELPIT which led me to what I thought was a brilliant deduction of HEAVEHO for “the shaft”. HELL before OVEN and CRIPES before CRIKEY.

I imagine we will get a lot of hollering about trivia today and proper nouns—remember, it is a Saturday. I also imagine there will be a few Naticks for some although everything was close to my wheelhouse in at least one direction or another—CREEL and CDRIVE was the closest I had to one today, as I don’t know what a CREEL is but I was pretty sure CDRIVE was the main one.

And finally I expect our friends overseas may find some of the Americana a stretch. I can visualize the mind of one of my good buddies here exploding already at CHCHCHCHIA. And to that I say, nobody from Poland should be complaining about a lack of vowels.

I see I'm good company in thinking CD something and not knowing the first letter of Billy Bud's captain's name. CRIKEY, it's C DRIVE.  I never read the book.
I do like the word HALCYON and do wonder how the non-US solvers will do with 1 Across.
Anyways, a KAC attack is always fun to solve.  Thanks you, Kameron.

Just a little faster than my Saturday average, though I thought I might get stumped by the NW section. When it all fell into place, I stared at 1A, baffled, until I realized what "The Gift That Grows" must be (I assume this refers to a TV commercial for it that I've never seen).

Pretty hard, very fair, and fairly fast (for me).  I knew 1 across immediately but it took me most of the puzzle to get it spelled as the constructor desired.  My left side was fairly barren until I got through the upper right.

A lot of near teeth pulling and yet magically pulling stuff out of dusty brain corners.  Oh, Savoy, I've heard of that theater name.  Okay, poem name makes sense.  Sluglike creature's not another eel, eh?  Not a garage sale but...

Just the right amount of slack and crosses for me to get through this.  XWStats shows "hard" which tracks for me.

A nice Saturday (for a change)!
Yes! Clue-bully KAC is back, thank goodness. Hard to believe 46D is a debut entry (or is it?). It made me feel 10 years old again.

After complaining all week about The Great Easening, I found today to be a real workout! I had to look up two clues; BON and UPPERVOLTA. I was never going to get them on my own. A few too many trivia and proper noun clues for my taste; but a good, hard puzzle.

CHA-CHA-CHA-CHIA.....no.
CHI-CHI-CHI-CHIA.....no.
CH-CH-CH-CHIA.....ah.
what a masterpiece. LOVED getting 1A without crosses. Try not to step on any VELVET WORMs while you're Stompin' at the SAVOY (Benny Goodman swing hit, 1936)
Thanks Wikipedia!
Very enjoyable.  Nice work!
So it turns out that Dian Fossey is no relation to Bob Fosse.

https://youtu.be/tzY7qQFij_M I'm heading down to my local K-Mart or Woolworth's right now to snag one of these: I hope they're still open this late. 😉 Never having seen this ad before made the top-left corner a bit of a quagmire for me, but I would expect no less from KAC — Bravo!
Fun puzzle. Loved 1A! Wonder if Velvet Worm is a mischievous wink at the knowledge that we'll all be hearing that ch ch.. earworm all day!
HET up... is it highly regional? Or crosswordese? This one was new for me. Thank you, crosses
Was well and truly stumped by Fort HAYS and IRENEPAPAS. Fun crossword, nevertheless.

Proud of myself for completing this one despite having never heard of some important answers, including 1A and 30A (funny, though). I finished the puzzle, typed CHCHCHCHIA into a search engine, watched a video, and waited for a memory bell to ring. Nope--missed that fad completely.

I wanted 19A, "Cookie, e.g." to be DESSERT, but I knew it wouldn't be and didn't waste graphite on it. Admittedly I ate too much chocolate cake while plugging away. Ate my cake but didn't have that answer, too.

Does the VELVET WORM perform at the SAVOY? I guess that was the Velvet Underground, maybe. Almost the same!

Enjoyed VERE much despite all.

I should have know.  I really should have.

A day after I post about a puzzle being easy, I get a real run for my money...I almost gave up several times.

I got the SE quadrant first, which is generally a sign I'm struggling.

But the last to fall was the NW, which was almost completely empty, other than my having "stye" for 1D, which didn't help at all.

After racking my brain to come up with Dr. Doolittle I realized AESOP was even better.

The head slap came with YOUAREHERE and TRACKER for 15A and 19A, which finally, finally, finally showed up in my head.  Then it was only a matter of sussing out IRENEPAPAS.  The name now rings a bell, but I was never going to recall it without practically everything else confidently in place.

Excellent puzzle!  A ton of fun.  A hold of gold.

1A is going to be one of those "love it or hate it" clue/answer pairs, I'm guessing.  

Well done, Cameron.  Very well done.

Very satisfying. I didn’t get last week’s without checking the puzzle (50 day streak gone just like that womp womp). I probably wouldn’t have gotten this puzzle in the print edition, what without the jingle to tell me I had finished it, the online version is somewhat more forgiving.

Saturday.  

Learned some more.  Enjoy the fall colors, stay safe from the floods, and may your crossword keep you humble.
This had  too many proper noun answers to be enjoyable, especially in the SE corner.

Wow, that was what you call a doozy! Maybe even a doozy of a LULU of a doozy!! Hooooweee!! Huzzah!! Very satisfying!!

Loads of fun! Loads of terrificly clued entries! ESTATE SALE, STRESS EATS, AVID READER, BATARANGS, CHCHCHCHIA, IDOS...  To name only a handful that I thought were terrific. 

Granted, I could have lived without BARFS, especially crossing STRESS EATS.....  CRIKEY 😬, but my oh so delicate sensibilities and I can live with it for getting such a fine puzzle. 😏

I never share my times, but today was so incredibly slow that I am extra not sharing it!  Har!!
“HAS” in clue list and answers.

Fun puzzle. Was very confused on ch-ch-ch-c—- until I figured out IRENE. Such a fun a-ha moment. I also had no idea who Dian Fossey was so I looked her up on Wikipedia. Wow, what a woman and what a life! Really unfortunate about her untimely and mysterious murder though.

Just started the puzzle, so not looking through the comments yet, but just wanted to crow for a second about filling in 1A immediately before anything else, figuring I'd probably have to change it, and it's right!
Challenging. Enjoyed it.

It took 30 minutes, which is roughly my Saturday average, but I managed to solve the puzzle after what I considered a valiant struggle. Or so I thought. Even though everything looked good, I got the dreaded "So close" pop-up. I checked and double checked my grid but I couldn't see any obvious errors. Feeling lost, I decided to consult the answer key.

My error turned out to be going for eLSA as the classic film character, which resulted in having BALDeSt for "Not all there upstairs?" - it sort of made sense. I have no idea what any Kansas fort is called, so I accepted tAYS without question (it certainly wouldn't be the strangest American place name I've seen in these puzzles). Ultimately then, as usual, it was the trivia that defeated me.

I generally enjoyed the solve. I found it challenging but doable, and I thought the misdirection was spot on. Knowing BATARANGS, PAPAS (even if I had her as Maria initially), models of VOLVOS, and __ER VOLTA (I relied for crosses to remind me if it was lowER or UPPER) helped a lot. Had I known less of today's trivia, I'd have needed lookups and reveals, probably.

The CHCHCHCHIA thing was a bit ridicuIous, no?

Could somebody please explain 'All worked (up)" solving to HET to me? I don't get it. What is HET?

Btw, we spell AESOP Ezop in Polish. Learning alternative spellings of names I've known for decades is among the biggest challenges of solving crossword puzzles in another language.
That was a fun, fair ride. And Fort Hays, who wouldn't know that!

fun challenge today thanks Kameron - I find it hard to believe this wasn't assisted by a.i. - that doesn't diminish all the good things in the puzzle - can the Times make it clear no a.i. was used to find the answers or clues?  other publications show 'powered by puzzle me' some do some don't.  I love the idea no steroid crosswords much like sports where the players are tested and can't compete if they're on 'extra help'.  analogy being I always thought of the Times as non 'GMO' puzzle and that's what makes it so endearing to all of us.  happy Saturday!

I opened the puzzle, scanned it, and delightedly wrote in Irene Papas, the brilliant actress I'd seen on my first date with my husband.  We had both been secretly trying to negotiate an opening for a relationship more connected than chatting while he painted my kitchen. (My roommate had moved out a couple of weeks before, to move in with the man she ultimately married.

Anyhow, my current relationship was not going well, there was this gorgeous man on a ladder in my kitchen, who talked literature and poetry while he expertly prepared and smoothed enamel on the cabinets over the sink, and the theater was only a block or two from my apartment.  "If you've read 'Electra,' you really need to see this movie." That was sixty years ago, and I still think Irena Papas was terrific.

Then I started the rest of the puzzle and got nowhere.  In desperation, I looked up a couple of names I'd never seen before and the iceberg started to melt.  The ChChChChia fell into place, but the creel had to be salvaged from sreel, which I had pretended might be some kind of fancy trap on a reel.  Anyway, I thought a creel was something you hauled the dead fish around in. (Column to the rescue.)  Each part of the puzzle was engaging and witty, but the proper names were both my nemesis and my salvation. 

Thank you, Kameron.  This one was a monumental Saturday workout.
Looking forward to imbibing the molten hatred spewed by foreign, younger and anti-brand-name solvers which will be generated by 1A.

Regarding the Midi, has Mr. Sivakumar invented some new version of Tic Tac Toe which involves the letters "p" "n" and "y?"

It is just the Midi, after all, but what am I missing?

Fun Saturday, one of those ones that felt hopeless at the beginning and I kept chipping away til it was done. The chia thing tripped me up for a while, having no clue about it, and sublimate was brilliant. At one point for the message with pointer I had ouija board! Well it fit… last to fall was Hays because baldism seemed to work since baldies and balding didn’t. Sneaky. Very enjoyable.

I hacked and slashed at it from the bottom up, somehow ending up with a completed puzzle when I got to the top. Excited that my college chemistry classes came in handy when I knew SUBLIMATES. A very cool thing to know, it's when something goes straight from solid to gas without stopping to be a liquid first. At least that's my recollection.

19A [Cookie, e.g.] TRACKER Here's a movie about a different kind of TRACKER. It's called "Point Last Seen" and stars Linda Hamilton. It's about a woman who learns to track people in the desert. You must start with the "point last seen." A fascinating and informative study of this skill. https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0177119/ https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/books/97/06/22/reviews/970622.22wilkint.html

Overall a fun puzzle from Kameron A.C. but the BAR(E/F)S ambiguity crossing with DIAN(E/F)OSSEY plus not knowing Kansas's Fort HAYS led to some look ups in the SE corner. I hate having to resort to look ups and I will be taking this out on my family later, 2/5 Grant R. Stars

Yes, yes, 1A was impossible.  I'm not sure why it was described as 'guessable'! And trivia "lovely"? I think of trivia (for me BOW, VOLVOS) as very tedious.
(Which holidays are 'approaching'? We have none until Christmas Day). 

CREEL is /was a well-known word in Scotland. It was used as a measure for the herring catch, and there was also a 'cran'. A wonderful book set around the herring fishing is "The Silver Darlings" by Neil Gunn. 

Otherwise, lots of clever clues, quite a few unknown to me but I expect that.

Geology moment! Glaciers SUBLIMATE in the sun and dry air of cold climes. The water changes from solid ice to water vapor without passing through the liquid phase. I had no idea of the word origin, though, that was interesting.

Maybe I'm the only person alive who says HET routinely. I guess it's part of my folksy charm ;). Context would be telling a story that involved stress about something. "Because of that, I was all het up, so maybe wasn't thinking straight..." 

Many sticky spots, some of which shouldn't have been so sticky, like CDRIVE, but I kept seeing CD in there. Also had BALDIng for a while, but Fort Gays (!!) ended that with a laugh.

It’s really annoying that the editors think “bao” is the Chinese word for steamed bun.   It is not.   Bao means many things but not that (for example bag or full).  A steamed bun is a baozi.    You can look it up in a dictionary if you don’t think this is the case.

A good chewy Saturday filled in near the Ethiopian/South Sudanese border drinking fine Ethiopian coffee. 
Having arrived a few weeks ago from Rwanda the Dian Fossey clue helped a lot. 
Travel broadening the mind eh?
Proud to have got 1A instantly…. And then proceeded to take an hour to solve the rest!

Finished by hook or by crook. Tough mix of the obscure, the esoteric, and (1 across) downright recondite!

There was nothing fun in this solve and no interesting new words I'll be adding to my vocab. Nevertheless, it was a good Saturday puzzle. 

Suppose not all puzzles can be enjoyable. Some just need to challenge 'the little grey cells'.
Not sure how I finished this one, but I did leave 46D with one blank square until the end, really not wanting to fill that in. Tough puzzle.
I thought 1A would be made up of actual notes and it also had 10 letters. But to my extreme disappointment.

KAMERON’S BACK!!!! 
Always a pleasure.

Tough one! I'm taking a break, hopefully my subconscious will be working on it while I do something else. Is that how it works? The NW is giving me fits. I've got a new puzzle on Crosshare, it's a themeless clued to be a quick solve with a few aha! moments. https://crosshare.org/PeatynOaty
A real lulu!
Steady climb but got it done.  BALDISH is a term used by no one, even when it applies to me.
Excellent, fill and cluing.  Thank you!

KAC is back! Not quite as tough as I hoped it would be, but we're getting there. Maybe a perfect Friday? Somehow, I had never heard the jingle and suspiciously eyed it as it began to emerge. Now, all I can think of is David Bowie: https://youtu.be/BPPSu0vaNWA?si=13VypxKvJxAOoI8B Initially, I misspelled ERMA as iRMA and didn't know VERE, so I was looking at CD RI_I. It took longer than it should have to figure that out.

The joys of solving that go beyond just filling in boxes.

Long answers often bring that sterling moment where you’ve been stumped, but suddenly your brain sees the answer from the crosses. – basically a fist-pumping “Hah!”  With 12 tens today, lots of these pings for me. 

Beauteous answers warm the heart, make you feel good and provide calm through solving storms.  Today: NOTHING BUT! SUBLIMATES, CHCHCHCHIA! HALCYON!  BELIE!  

The buzz of newness excites the brain.  I’m not just talking about debut answers (eight today), but answers we’ve seen before clued differently, from a different angle or with new wordplay.

Then there are the memory triggers.  I flashed on Little LULU, a comic book character I haven’t thought about in decades.  Also the CHIA jingle and the Dead Sea, a magical place I visited long ago.

Your puzzles, Kameron, always bring these extras, and turn the solving experience from robotic, to an event.  More please, and thank you once again for a splendid outing!
This was painful and not in a good way

A KAC Saturday.

Life is good.

So, when I was in my early 20s, I visited the DEAD SEA.  I was by myself at the time, and everyone said to go and see it.  I really didn’t know anything about it.

When I arrived, I saw many people just standing in the water.  Hardly anyone was moving.  I just thought it was a stodgy crowd.

Back then, the way I liked to enter a lake or the ocean was to run full speed into the water, maybe even splash those nearby, and I was going to do that this time, and show these people what fun looks like.

What I didn’t know was that the water was so salty and mineral–rich,  you could actually sit on top of it.  That salt, if it splashes in your face, seriously sears the eyes.

So, as I began my run from a great distance from the sea’s lip, I could see the beginnings of looks of terror in the faces of those on the beach as well as in the water.  As I got closer, I saw their arms flailing, heard shouts of “NOOOOOO”.  It was like one of those slow motion sequences in a movie, with faces zoomed in on, and voices slow motion slow and low.

The people in the water turned their backs to me and covered their eyes.  People on the beach were running to stop my invasion of the water.

Oh, I got the message and stopped in time, but I will never forget that moment.  Hadn’t thought about it in forever.  But today when I uncovered DEAD SEA, it was as if I were there.

I wanted Dr Dolittle to fit (1967 Rex Harrison).   

Bon Iver, Justin Vernon, was a gimme - from Wisconsin.
I should’ve gotten 43D easily since I’m a VOLVO owner. I grew up in a 2000 S70, and now I drive a 2008 S80.

I hope this puzzle wasn't as traumatic for everyone else as it was for me. It was just last week my parents informed me that my little brother was actually a chia pet.

I can't help feeling like I should have known. At least now I understand why he was always their favorite.

Cripes! (or is it "Crikes!"?) It took me forever to rind that last mistake! Fun fact: Bon Iver took their name from the French phrase "Bon hiver!," ("Happy Winter!"), which is used as a greeting by the residents of Cicely, AK on the occasion of the first snowfall of the season, in the TV series *Northern Exposure*. Here is home-town girl Erma Franklin singing "Lied der Lulu" by Alban Berg: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rFEn0JQsy2w&list=RDrFEn0JQsy2w&start_radio=1 (Just wish--actually it's Barbara Hannigan, who also conducts!) Now off to read Aesop's fable "το Βελούδινο Σκουλήκι και το Κατοικίδιο Χία" ("The Velvet Worm and the Chia Pet")

Still working on the puzzle, but had to jump in here to note what a great clue and answer 1 Across are. When I got the first three letters from the downs, I briefly thought something was wrong, but then it suddenly clicked. Great puzzle yesterday and so far today!

CRIKEY! Tough one today, even though I was well below my average time.

Almost to the end I was suspicious that there were some rebuses I was missing. I was suspicious of my own answer for 9D because I always assumed that IRENE had another P in her last name.

I've never seen Casablanca, so I originally guessed ROSE, who I think is a character from another movie I've never seen, for 49D. Once I got 16A I figured she wasn't likely to appear twice.

Very nice use of improbable consonant strings to challenge us, not limited to 1A. There was a year I was tempted to get a CHIA Garcia, but I've not seen them on the market in a long time.

What Great Easening?
Never got into the swing of this one. Couldn’t shake the feeling that it was lying to me until I filled the last square.

I hated it more with every non-word. Gagged on "baldish," retched at "tented," and just snorted with horror at the clue "altarations." Never heard of "The Gift That Grows," and a jingle is a musical phrase, not a phonetic one. Ugh ugh ugh.
CREEL sems a bit archaic. I still got it though...

For me, a perfect puzzle because solved it with no look ups but didn’t know the answers to several clues without crosses. To the haters: isn’t that what you want? Learn a little but still find a solution? It’s a puzzle not a dictionary.

Congratulations!
You solved a Saturday
Crossword in 52:58.

Not much to add. A true Saturday workout for me. Got it without assistance, but had doubts right up until the end. BALDING rather than BALDISH slowed me down in the SE. VELVETWORM was a complete unknown. Didn't know the Greek actress, but PAPAS made a lot more sense than PEPAS, so my misspelled BATERANGS became BATARANGS just in the nick of time. 

More at this level of challenge, please.

That veiled lower-case ‘t’ at the start of the 1D clue had me frustrated for a long time, since I don’t know any of the big US department-surgery chains.

Otherwise, a very fun puzzle!
Colour me halcyon.
This felt like a classic puzzle in the worst way. Overused crossword cliches, out-dated references, just a 2/10 time all around.
There was some clever Wordplay in this, but too many of the clues made me groan when I got the answer so this wasn't my favourite sadly.

Fun puzzle, 2026 difficulty (which is to say, the level of clueing we’d see on Wednesdays in a slightly less dystopic timeline).

It’s funny how many people got 1A right off the bat. I grew up on TV at the time those commercials were running and remember that jingle quite clearly; but I totally forgot that tagline and initially had no idea what _genre_ of answer the clue was pointing at (lyrics? solfège notes? “tra la la” kinda thing?).

Anyhoo, there was at least some fun clueing. Personal highlights: AVIDREADER, COP, and ESTATESALE.
Going through the alphabet to figure out a clue is  SOP for me.
HET? How do I still remember the Chia commercials from the 80s but I’ve never heard of HET?

Good Saturday workout. Just got stuck in a couple places and couldn't quite work it all out. No big deal. And... puzzle find today: A Sunday from August 9, 1998 by Christopher Hurt with the title: "Vicious Circle." Not easy to describe this one. Several noted writers - straightforwardly clued and place in various sections all around the puzzle. e.g... FRANKLINPADAMS EDNAFERBER GEORGEKAUFMAN ROBERTBENCHLEY and, several others. But then the 'reveal,' clued as... "Where the smart set sat (answer to be entered in the appropriate manner)" And that answer was entered... across and then down, and then back across and up. i.e. a 'square'. ATTHEAL/GONQUI/NROUN/DTABLE Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=8/9/1998&h=118a You need to look at it to really get it. I'm done. ...

Ah, yes ...'Starry VERE' from Billy Budd.  Knew that would come in handy someday -- it just took 48 years.  The fruits of a liberal arts education.

Natick alert in the SE:  Dian, we're not in Kansas anymore.  25 turns on the alphabet wheel for the gold star.

Awesome puzz.

So fun to get CHCHCHCHIA from the off, then shift to the NW downs to verify and have them all fall with NOTHINGBUT the toehold of that 1A. Kam, when can we expect a clue for Sea-Monkeys? Amusing to think of BALDISH in the context of an early growth stage of that outré Chia Pet spin-off, the Chia Head. DIAN FOSSEY, you saved my SE corner. Now you’re even more my hero. And in homage to another “Phenomenal WOMAN,” here's a link to Maya Angelou's poem and her reading of it: https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/04/04/maya-angelou-recites-phenomenal-woman/
“Who is General Failure, and why is he reading my C-Drive?”
HET for all worked up?  Is that initials for something?.
Can’t remember when I was so pleased with myself for a clean solve! I did not think I was going to get it but it fell like Cuban dominoes in the end.

1A escaped me for the longest time and was the last to fall but no lookups! One quibble, I think of a creel as a small wicker basket with a lid that was hung from the shoulder and used to carry one’s trout. Don’t really see it as a trap but someone please correct me if I’m wrong.

I struggled with the NW corner, because the chia pet jingle was not familiar. Not one of the memorable commercials of my youth. I tend to think of things like "you're soaking in it" for Palmolive.

I've never been a fan of KAC's puzzles, but this one was better than most for me.
This one had me thoroughly stuck as I couldn’t remember 1A , even though I had an Albert Einstein Chia pet!   Great puzzle!

Goodness that felt hard, though I managed to complete only just over my average time. I’ve never heard of 1A so that wasn’t a great start. I stuttered on, saved only by the gimmes of Ms Angelou and the amazing DIAN FOSSEY. I read her autobiography as a teen I think, which would have been the mid 70’s. I recall being so struck by this determined young woman, who knew exactly what she wanted to do, at a time when I had no clue where my life was going. I mean, it wasn’t to hare into the rainforests looking for gorillas, but still…
Everything else fell very slowly. Too many TILs to name. The WORM sounds like something out of a horror film.
Chuckled when I finally got STRESS EATS.
All in all a decent Saturday grid I think, perhaps too much of a slog to love it, but that’s on me.

I was having a good time doing this puzzle, and, at about the 13 minute mark, only had the southeast corner to go. Ended at over 20 minutes. Baldish, Dian Fossey, and plenty others got filled in eventually, but very slowly. Still a good puzzle overall.

BALDISH is a word. By all that's right and holy, it shouldn't be, but it is. It's right there, in Merriam Webster, along with a quote.

The "I" in it was the last to fall. As the music played I was sitting slumped on the couch, my mouth open a bit, staring at the screen and blinking.
Laughed out loud when I realized chchchchia had to be the answer. You have to have a great sense of humor to start a puzzle with that! Nice work, Kameron.

Very chewy for me.  Got stuck on 30A because I was so sure they had to be RINGS and I thought Ms Angelou could have used WOMIN though on reflection that isn't like her.
  And since I had a couple of letters, I thought 26D was going to be some variation on our good friend EEL. Then I got enough crosses near the end to see WORM. But still kinda sad to give it up.

The most difficult puzzle for me that I’ve seen on this site in many a year, and I mean that as a compliment. 

I still remember learning about Ouagadougou, the capital of Upper Volta, in tenth grade to play a geography game. I remember, too, when Upper Volta changed its name to Burkina Faso. But it was only today that I learned why the country changed its name to split from its French colonial past. Burkina Faso meaning “incorruptible homeland “, combining Mossi and Dyula etymology.

This puzzle was very tough, until it suddenly wasn't. The top half was pretty much empty on first pass, then the middle fell and with that the entire puzzle gave way. It's so curious how these late week puzzles play out in so many different ways.

A tougher Saturday for me, partially because I did it without benefit of coffee or pastry. I finally had to look up DIAN FOSSEY to find out her last name didn't end with IE. After that, things made sense in the SE corner. I'm not familiar with the Chia Pet jingle, so that took a while - and HET? I got the gold star, so I guess it's correct. Oh well. Thanks for the fun!

In re: the VELVET WORM.
An absolutely fascinating creature. Far from "slug-like"-- the scientific name is Onychphora, or 'claw-bearing'-- velvet worms are actually related to tardigrades and arthropods. Their appendages and segmentation make them look sort of like centipede prototypes.
But they are different enough to be classified in their own Phylum. A fossil that is very similar in form to modern types is known from the early Cambrian, 500+ mya (though it was marine and all modern species are moist-terrestrial). They are insectivorous and indeed catch their prey by spitting an adhesive goo at them.
I saw one in the wild in Ecuador in 2009, and it was one of the greatest thrills among many on that trip. It's not often that one gets to add an entire Phylum to one's life list!

When I was a larval marine biologist, an advisor said a good way to create a niche was to become very well versed in a specific topic or taxon. At the time, I was set on becoming an invertebrate zoologist, and had a fascination with the onychophora, so I briefly decided I would become a VELVET WORM specialist. It was fairly easy to do so, since there was such limited literature on them... fortunately, I figured out soon thereafter that I really, really loved nudibranchs, and began learning all I could about the sea slugs of the Oregon intertidal, thereby un-restricting myself. 

I did later on do research on sea slugs, but not those -- smaller ones that lived in the tropics and subtropics, and, as I mentioned in these comments some months ago, the lovely temperate ones in the genus Elysia. 

I'm glad I did not take that advice and become so narrowly focused on a single obscure group. I have worked with invertebrates from many phyla, and even (shudder) a FISH once! (striped bass). It is the great diversity of fascinating and lovely critters among the invertebrates that has made a career in IZ so rewarding to me.
